name: Dark Green
lede: Dark Green is the web color `#006400`, a deep, saturated green defined for the X11 and CSS color lists, and also the name of a whole family of darker greens.

sections.title: One swatch, three systems
sections.body:
The swatch is the web color `darkgreen`, `#006400`, one of the colors in the X11 set [1]. It has no pigment behind it: red and blue are switched off and the green channel is set to 100 of 255 [9]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the swatch as a deep yellowish green, block 137, almost exactly (a color distance of 0.7) [9].

The older systems that carry the same name are much greyer. Ridgway's 1912 plate gives a dark green that, as scanned from an aged plate, is closer to `#4B6A56`, and the XKCD color survey of 2010 produced two quite different answers, `#033500` and `#054907` [9]. So "dark green" is a family and not a place. The nearest names to the web swatch in our library are [[deep-green]], [[tree-green]] and [[forest-green]], and the standard cousins are [[racing-green]] and [[sap-green]] [9].

sections.title: Dark greens with their own names
sections.body:
English has many names for a dark green when it needs to be exact. Paterson gives *loden*, after the cloth; *racing green*, the dark green of British racing cars of the 1920s; *épinard*, the dark green of spinach; and *invisible green*, so dark that it verges on black [2]. He also lists *Jenkin's green*, a name for a dark green made with amorphous carbon, and *verde eterno*, a dark green pigment of Venetian painters [2]. *Pine* and *nettle* can name dark greens too [2].

The dark end of the family was dyed from plants as well. Finlay reports that in the Outer Hebrides tweed mill she visited, dark green came from teasels [8].

sections.title: A dark color for serious people
sections.body:
The Greek word *prasinos*, literally leek-colored, began to compete with older green words from the third or second century BCE and covered all the strong shades of green, especially the dark ones [3]. Dark green had a gloomy side in the Middle Ages [12]. Pastoureau notes that images of the Virgin from before the twelfth century show her in dark colors that include dark green, which signified mourning [12]. In fifteenth-century French poetry, a "lost green" is one of three colors of sorrow and death, with black and tan [4].

It also marked a line between the sober and the worldly. Pastoureau recounts that Racine, in his short worldly period in the early 1660s, scandalized his patrons at Port-Royal by turning up in a very dark green suit, when only black was acceptable [5]. By the French Enlightenment, people who had always worn black began to wear gray, brown, blue or dark green instead [6].

sections.title: What it pairs with
sections.body: Gage notes that nineteenth-century color theorists, Helmholtz and Rood among them, held that a bright purplish red is the complement of dark green [7]. That is one tradition's rule of thumb, and other systems of complements give other answers.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of this swatch fills at least five per cent of the canvas in only 5 of 23,781 paintings, and it is rarer than 79 per cent of the named colors [10]. The earliest hit is [[painting:aic-16327|Jean Hey's *The Annunciation*]] of about 1490, with later hits in 1825 and 1895, including [[painting:nga-43713|*Aurora*, an American picture of 1825]] [10]. That date is 422 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, so the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph and not proof of a dye [10].

In Google Books the phrase *dark green* peaks in the 1930s [11]. As always, screen colors are approximate and the archive is photographs of varnished paintings [10].
